College of Education and Professional Studies Proposed PhD Program Curriculum Total Number of Required Credits= 60 Credits (post-Master’s Degree) Curricular Overview Core sequence (12 credits) Research methods (21 credits) Dissertation Preparation and Credits (12 credits) Advanced Electives/Focused Expertise (15 credits) CORE/Foundational Courses (12 Credits total) ● EDP 600 Academic Reading & Writing for Doctoral Studies (3 cr)- Fall ● EDP 610 Contemporary Issues in Educational Inquiry (3 cr)- Fall ● EDP 611 Issues and Problems in Educational Inquiry (3 cr)- Spring ● EDP 622 Societal Perspectives of Education (3 cr)-Spring Research methods courses (21 credits total) ● EDP 623 Research Design (3 cr)- Fall ● EDP 612 Qualitative Research Methods in Education (3 cr)- Fall ● EDC 684 The Analysis of Data: A Hands-On [Qualitative] Approach (3 cr)- Spring ● EDP 613 Introduction to Quantitative Research (3 cr)-Fall ● EDC 624 Applied Educational Quantitative Data Analysis (3 cr)-Fall or Spring TBA ● EDC 625 [New] Engaged Research Apprenticeship in Education (3 cr)-Fall or Spring TBA ● Plus one additional advanced methods course.

Options include but are not limited to: ○ EDC 685 - Survey Design (3 cr) ○ EDC 682 - Discourse Analysis in Education Research (3 cr) ○ Any other advanced methods course at URI Dissertation Preparation and Research (12 credits minimum) ● EDP 641 Doctoral Dissertation Research Seminar (3 cr) - Fall and Spring ● EDP 699 Doctoral Dissertation Research (minimum 9 cr) - Fall and Spring Focused Expertise (15 credits minimum) Students have the opportunity to use 15 credits to delve deeply into a focus area that aligns with their career goals.
With support from their faculty mentor, students will select 15 credits of courses that best align with their scholarly trajectory.
With the goal of flexibility, students can design a program following any of the following paths: ● Courses selected from an area of education where we already have graduate programming (e.g., Elementary, Secondary, Higher Education/CSP, Adult Education, TESOL/BDL, Reading, Health and Physical Education (HPE).

● Courses that focus on topic areas that cut across current programs to illuminate complex, cross-cutting issues.
For instance, students could focus on Language, Literacy, and Culture where they could combine courses to develop expertise across areas such as: TESOL and bilingual education, digital and arts-based literacies, reading, and dyslexia.
A second option would be to focus on “postsecondary education leadership, learning and development” and combine pre-existing courses in education policy, college student personnel, and adult education. ● Courses combined with independent study to focus on a particular educational niche.
Like many other fields students, can opt to work with a SOE scholar to develop a narrowly tailored focus that aligns with one or more faculty experts in the college (e.g., STEM education, Social Justice Education, etc.).
URI CATALOG DESCRIPTIONS EDP 600 Academic Reading & Writing for Doctoral Studies (3 crs.) Students develop and practice academic reading, writing, and thinking skills involved in professional practices of educational research and publishing communities.

Course emphasizes scholarly identity and writing cogent literature reviews. (Lec. 2, Sem 1) EDP 610 Contemporary Issues in Educational Inquiry (3 crs.) Examination of issues and problems related to philosophical and historical aspects of educational thought and the role of society.
Empirical analysis of classroom settings is emphasized. (Seminar) EDP 611 Issues and Problems in Educational Inquiry (3 crs.) Examination of issues and problems related to philosophical and historical aspects of educational thought and the role of society.
Empirical analysis of classroom setting is emphasized. (Seminar) EDP 612 Qualitative Research Methods in Education (3 crs.) Survey of qualitative methods of educational research: terminology, historical development, assumptions, and models of inquiry.
EDP 613 Introduction to Quantitative Research (4 crs.) Educational research data are collected, quantitatively analyzed and interpreted.
Applications of the general linear model to a variety of research designs and analytic strategies are emphasized. (Lec. 3, Rec. 1) EDP 622 Societal Perspectives of Education (3 crs.) Application of theory to the intersection of community service, academic

EDP 623 Research Design (3 crs.) Research design process including developing problem statements, research questions, hypotheses and appropriate methods (i.e., qualitative, quantitative, or mixed).
Course considers philosophical worldviews, literature reviews, theory use, and research ethics. (Lec. 3) EDP 641 Doctoral Dissertation Research Seminar (1 cr.) Bi-weekly forums present evolving research questions and empirical designs.
Discussion and feedback refine individuals' research plan, enhancing the methodological perspectives and tools of all participants. (Seminar) EDC 682 - Discourse Analysis in Education Research (3 crs.) The analysis of discourse in educational research is examined and practiced in this course.

Students conduct various analyses of discourse samples and explore a variety of analytic research frameworks. (Seminar 3) EDC 684 - The Analysis of Data: A Hands-On Approach (3 crs.) Students will practice data analysis using three specific qualitative methodologies, noting that each of these methodologies offers a unique lens on phenomena. (Seminar 3) EDC685 - Survey Design (3 crs.) Principles, theories, techniques, and applications for developing survey questionnaires and conducting survey research in education; developing questions; constructing instruments; implementing surveys; reducing coverage and sampling errors. (Seminar 3) EDP 699 Doctoral Dissertation Research (1-12 crs.) Number of credits is determined each semester in consultation with the major professor or program committee. (Independent Study) S/U only.
NOTES: Some of the pre-requisites on these pre-existing courses may need to be revised.
CEPS will make those minor changes in 2024/2025 to allow the current Joint PhD program students to enroll seamlessly during the teach out of that program.

Rationale for closing program: In 1993, the University of Rhode Island entered into a partnership with Rhode Island College to offer a Joint PhD program in Education.
Although the intention was for the universities to share the responsibility (budget, staffing, etc.), Rhode Island College has not, in recent years, been in a position to support half of the program responsibilities.
As such, the program has largely been supported by URI (teaching faculty, graduate assistants, travel funding, etc.).
Yet, most of the tuition revenue has flowed to Rhode Island College.

The individual who serves as panel advisor shall not be the person who conducted the original investigation as described in 9.20.10 and 9.21.10.

The staff of the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office may defer conduct action at any stage of the process for a period not to exceed ninety calendar days when school is in session.
Pending charges may be discontinued thereafter depending upon the good conduct of the accused student. #04-05–32 9.21.31 Conduct Records.
All conduct records, such as complaint letters, correspondence, charge letters, decision letters, and hearing summaries, shall be considered confidential, and be maintained by the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office for six years after the date of the action.
Records of unresolved incidents shall be reviewed annually starting with the 6-year anniversary.
The Dean of Students shall decide whether or not to destroy such a record or keep it for another year.

Access to such records is governed by the University Policies for the Release and Disclosure of Information from Student Records (see section 6.12.21). #04-05–32 9.24.11 Appeal on the Issue of Off-Campus Jurisdiction.

If a student is accused of an off-campus offense under subsection 2 of Section 9.24.10, and if the representative of the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office determines that there is cause for presenting the matter to the Student Discipline System, the student shall have the right to dispute the jurisdiction of the Student Discipline System.
Such an appeal must be filed in writing with the Office of Student Life not later than three days after notice of the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office decision that the student has been charged.
The appeal shall be presented to the Vice President for Student Affairs for disposition of the issue of jurisdiction.
The decision on jurisdiction arrived at by the Vice President for Student Affairs shall be final.
When an affirmative judgment on jurisdiction has been reached through this procedure, the student shall still have the right to accept or deny responsibility for the conduct in question. 9.25.10 Mediation.

When there is an apparent violation of community standards or University policies for students, the incident may be adjudicated through a formal mediation process if formal mediation is acceptable to all of the following parties: (1) the individual(s) allegedly responsible for the violation; (2) the complainant (student, staff or department reporting the violation), and (3) the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office .
Mediation shall be conducted by a trained University staff member approved by the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office .
Mediation requires the cooperation of all parties to resolve a problem.
The process is to result in a written document agreed to by all parties.
The written agreement shall be kept on file in the Office of Student Life Dean of Students Office .
Should Mediation fail to result in an agreement, or should a party fail to abide by an agreement, formal disciplinary proceedings shall then be initiated.

CONSTITUTION, BY-LAWS, AND UNIVERSITY MANUAL COMMITTEEReport #2022-2023-20 - Report on Certificates and MinorsFACULTY SENATE - May 4, 2023 Context: Policies relating to Undergraduate Certificates and Minors A disagreement in the interpretation of UM language about minors between representatives of adegree-granting college and representatives from Enrollment Services was referred to FSEC andCBUM.
FSEC charged CBUM with examining the policies relating to minor fields of study andUndergraduate Certificate Programs, as they are codified in the UM, and to bring forthrecommendations to the Faculty Senate.
This report includes proposed editorial changes to the UMand aims to: 1) resolve the ambiguity in current UM language and clarify policies governingUndergraduate Certificate Programs, 2) increase clarity and comprehensibility in the current UMlanguage about Minor fields of study, and 3) report on the need to resolve confusion and conflictinginterpretations of language in UM 8.20.52.

The disagreement stemmed from confusion in UM 8.20.52 about the total number of courses andcredits that students may apply to different degree requirements, including the major field of studyand the minor field of study: - “A maximum of two courses required in a major program may be used to apply to both the major and minor fields of study.” - “Courses from other curricula that are recommended or required for the major may apply to the minor.” - “Courses in General Education may be used for the minor.” The members of CBUM examined and discussed this language that has been interpreted in differentways and agree that, while there are no limits on the number of General Education courses thatstudents may also apply to the minor, the maximum number of courses that may be applied to boththe major and minor fields of study is two, and this limit applies to all courses that students apply tothe major field of study, regardless of course code and including “courses from other curricula thatare recommended or required for the major.” CBUM understands that some faculty and department chairs have interpreted this confusing UMlanguage on minors more broadly and believed that it was permissible to apply to both the major andminor fields of study 1) a maximum of two courses from the major program (courses carrying thecourse code of the major program of study), and 2) an unlimited number of courses from othercurricula (different course codes).

Upon further investigation and deliberation, CBUM discovered thatone of the fundamental differences between Undergraduate Certificates and Minors revolves aroundthe precise issue of the level of flexibility in applying credits to both the major field of study and theother area of inquiry: Undergraduate Certificate Programs have no limits, minors have limits.
In addition to the following three (3) proposals for editorial changes to the UM, CBUM refers to theCurriculum and Standards Committee the broader issue of establishing clarity in the curricularstandards for Minor programs, and determining if it would be advisable to bring forth additionallanguage to clarify the distinctions between Undergraduate Certificates and Minors.

Proposal 1: Editorial changes to clarify UM language on Undergraduate Certificates Rationale: Editorial clarifications to UM language on the nature of Undergraduate CertificatePrograms and on the policies governing the process by which students earn an UndergraduateCertificate.
Existing language: 8.20.73 Courses completed in pursuit of an Undergraduate Certificate may be used to apply toward undergraduate degree requirements.
Undergraduate Certificate courses may not be taken under the pass-fail grading option.
Applicants may not transfer courses into an undergraduate Certificate Program that have been taken at institutions other than URI.
Credits earned at URI and applied to the Undergraduate Certificate Program must have been taken within eight years of matriculating into the Undergraduate Certificate Program and cannot total more than two-fifths of the total number of credits required for the Undergraduate Certificate Program. #16-17-22 Proposed changes: 8.20.73 All Cc ourses completed in pursuit of an Undergraduate Certificate may be used to apply toward undergraduate degree requirements.

Some degree programs consist of multiple certificate programs that, when combined or stacked, comprise many or all of the program’s degree requirements .
